content: Various antibiotics that can penetrate the central nervous system have been shown to be effective in killing Borrelia burgdorferi, the bacterium responsible for Lyme neuroborreliosis (LNB), both in laboratory and animal studies. These antibiotics are commonly used in clinical practice to treat LNB, but their comparative effectiveness remains unclear. To evaluate the effects of antibiotics in treating LNB, a systematic review was conducted. Searches were performed on October 25, 2016, in multiple databases, including the Cochrane Neuromuscular Specialised Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, and Embase. Clinical trial registries were also searched on October 26, 2016. Bibliographies of identified randomized trials were reviewed, and experts in the field were contacted to identify additional data. No language restrictions were applied during the search. The review included randomized clinical trials that compared any antibiotic treatment, including combination therapies, against other treatments, placebo, or no treatment in adults and children with LNB. Studies focusing on post-Lyme syndrome were excluded. Standard Cochrane methodological procedures were used for data collection and analysis. Seven randomized studies involving 450 European participants with LNB were included in the review. No trials conducted in the United States were identified. Significant variability among the studies prevented a meta-analysis. None of the studies included a placebo control for the initial antibiotic treatment, and only one study was blinded. None of the trials used a delayed-start design. All studies were active comparator trials, and most were underpowered to detect non-inferiority. The antibiotics investigated included penicillin G and ceftriaxone (in four studies), doxycycline (in three studies), and cefotaxime (in two studies). One study compared a three-month course of oral amoxicillin to placebo following initial intravenous ceftriaxone treatment. One study focused exclusively on children. The trials used diverse outcome measures, including physicianor patient-reported outcomes, and in some cases, cerebrospinal fluid analysis as an indirect biomarker of disease and treatment response. None of the studies reported on the primary outcome proposed by the review, which was long-term improvement in overall disability (measured at three months or more). No significant differences in symptom resolution were observed between treatment groups in response to active antibiotic therapy. Overall, the treatments were generally well-tolerated, but the quality of adverse event reporting was poor. The authors concluded that the available evidence is of low to very low quality, derived from a small number of heterogeneous trials with inconsistent outcome measures. These studies lacked sufficient power and did not use standardized entry criteria or efficacy endpoints. As a result, it is not possible to draw definitive conclusions about the relative efficacy of different central nervous system-penetrant antibiotics for treating LNB. Most patients experienced good outcomes, with symptoms resolving within 12 months regardless of the antibiotic used. However, a minority of patients did not improve adequately and required retreatment. The studies provided some evidence supporting the efficacy of doxycycline, penicillin G, ceftriaxone, and cefotaxime in treating European LNB. No additional benefit was observed in one study where initial intravenous ceftriaxone treatment was followed by prolonged oral amoxicillin therapy. There is a lack of high-quality evidence on the efficacy of antibiotics for treating LNB in the United States.
